title: Distance-Vector vs Link-State Routing
summary: Compare the two classic intra-domain routing algorithm families — how each builds its routes, where each breaks, and why link-state largely won for anything beyond small networks.

slides.sectionTitle: Two ways to build a routing table
slides.markdown: Within a single administrative network, routers need to learn routes automatically rather than being hand-configured for every destination. Two classic families solve this: **distance-vector** (share your table with your neighbors) and **link-state** (share your own links with everyone, then compute the map yourself).

In **distance-vector** routing, each router periodically shares its *entire* routing table with its directly-connected neighbors — "here's every destination I know, and my cost to reach it." A neighbor updates its own table if a received route is cheaper than what it already has, then passes its updated table on.

No router ever sees the full network topology — it only ever knows "neighbor X says it can reach destination Y at cost Z," trusting that secondhand information rather than computing anything from a complete map.

**RIP (Routing Information Protocol)** is the textbook distance-vector protocol: its metric is simply **hop count** (number of routers traversed), and it caps at **15 hops** — 16 means "unreachable."

This simplicity is also RIP's ceiling: hop count ignores actual link speed or congestion (a 1-hop satellite link counts the same as a 1-hop fiber link), and the 15-hop cap makes RIP unusable on any network with a longer diameter. It's rarely deployed in serious production networks today, but it's the cleanest example to learn the distance-vector mechanism from.

Distance-vector's biggest weakness: when a route goes down, neighbors can keep telling each other stale information, each incrementing the cost, until it slowly counts up to "infinity":

![A stale route bouncing between two routers, each incrementing the hop count, until it reaches the unreachable threshold](assets/count-to-infinity.svg)

**Split horizon** (never advertise a route back to where you learned it) and **poison reverse** (advertise it as unreachable back there) are the standard fixes, both built into RIP.

assets.alt: A stale route bouncing between two routers, each incrementing the hop count, until it reaches the unreachable threshold

slides.markdown:
In **link-state** routing, each router instead floods information about just its own direct links ("I'm connected to X and Y, at these costs") to *every* router in the area — not just its immediate neighbors. Every router ends up with an identical copy of the full **link-state database**, describing the entire topology.

Each router then independently computes its own routing table from that shared map — no secondhand trust involved, since every router is reasoning from the same complete picture.

With a full topology map in hand, each router runs **Dijkstra's algorithm** locally to compute the shortest path from itself to every other node — building its own routing table as the output.

Because every router runs the same algorithm over the identical database, they independently arrive at a mutually consistent view of the network, without needing to trust anyone else's computed result — only the raw link data, which they verified came directly from its source.

**OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)** is the dominant link-state protocol in enterprise networks. It divides a large network into **areas**, so link-state flooding stays contained within an area rather than overwhelming the whole network — a scalability fix link-state protocols specifically need, since flooding globally doesn't scale forever.

OSPF also converges far faster than RIP after a topology change, since routers react immediately to a flooded link-state update rather than waiting on periodic full-table exchanges.

slides.sectionTitle: Flooding vs table exchange, side by side
slides.markdown:
The core mechanical difference, visualized directly:

![Distance-vector routers exchanging full tables with only their immediate neighbors, versus link-state routers flooding their own link data to the whole area](assets/ls-vs-dv-exchange.svg)

Distance-vector shares a lot of (secondhand) information with a few neighbors; link-state shares a little (firsthand) information with everyone.

assets.alt: Distance-vector routers exchanging full tables with only their immediate neighbors, versus link-state routers flooding their own link data to the whole area

slides.markdown:
| | Distance-vector | Link-state |
|---|---|---|
| Info shared | Whole routing table, to neighbors only | Own links only, to everyone |
| Convergence | Slow — periodic updates, count-to-infinity risk | Fast — reacts immediately to flooded changes |
| Router overhead | Lower CPU (no Dijkstra), simpler | Higher CPU (Dijkstra per router), more complex |
| Scalability | Poor on large/complex topologies | Good, especially with areas (OSPF) |

**How to decide:** distance-vector's simplicity fits small, stable, low-complexity networks; link-state's overhead is worth paying the moment scale, convergence speed, or topology complexity actually matter — which is most production networks today.

**Convergence** is the state where every router in a network agrees on a consistent, correct view of the topology — after a link fails, a network is "converging" until every router's table reflects the new reality.

This matters operationally because packets can be dropped or looped **during** convergence, before all routers agree — the faster a protocol converges (link-state's core advantage over distance-vector), the shorter that window of inconsistent, potentially broken forwarding.

slides.subTitle: "The routing protocol should just pick the shortest physical path"
slides.markdown:
A common mistake is assuming a routing protocol picks the geographically or physically shortest path. It doesn't — it picks the path with the lowest value of whatever **metric** it's configured to use: hop count (RIP), a configurable cost often tied to bandwidth (OSPF), or something entirely policy-driven (BGP, covered next).

A 3-hop path over slow satellite links can lose to a 5-hop path over fast fiber, if the protocol's metric weighs bandwidth — "shortest" in routing almost always means "lowest metric," not "fewest physical kilometers."
